prompt.context: The maker of Botox is considering expanding to the migraine market and has already begun clinical trials in this area. The product is expected to receive FDA approval in 2016.
prompt.question: Your team has been hired to assess the viability of this product for launch. How will you determine if the market is attractive? If the market is attractive, do you have any recommendations regarding how to launch the product? What concerns should the client take into consideration before deciding to launch?

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of the drug?
clarifying_info.a: The drug will be priced at $200 per injection.
It is a prophylactic injection given every 2 months.

clarifying_info.q: What are the development and launch costs?
clarifying_info.a: Remaining development and launch costs amount to approximately $5B.
Manufacturing marginal costs are expected to be quite small.

clarifying_info.q: What is the annual marketing expense?
clarifying_info.a: Annual marketing expense can be estimated at $1B.

clarifying_info.q: How does the product compare to existing treatments?
clarifying_info.a: It offers similar efficacy compared to the market leading option but without any side effects. It also has some added skin care benefits.
The market leading branded prescription oral migraine treatment lost patent protection last year. There is also a strong over-the-counter generic market for migraine treatments.

clarifying_info.q: What share of migraine sufferers are willing to try the medicine?
clarifying_info.a: Assume at least 10% of migraine sufferers are willing to try such a medicine.
This drug will initially be produced in the US, so use US population of 300 million.

clarifying_info.q: What share of the market can Botox capture?
clarifying_info.a: Due to the absence of side effects and the beneficial skin care properties, assume 20%-40% of the overall market in 5 years.

framework: Market sizing: estimate the size and revenue potential of the migraine prescription market
Product assessment: evaluate product attributes, pricing, and fit for the target population
Competitive analysis: assess current competition and Botox's differentiation
Launch considerations: identify risks, regulatory hurdles, branding concerns, and cannibalization
Recommendation: synthesize findings into a go/no-go recommendation with proposed launch strategy

questions.prompt: Size the US prescription migraine market in annual revenue dollars.
questions.guidance: Walk through a bottom-up market sizing: US population → % chronic migraine sufferers → % with severe migraines needing prescription treatment → annual revenue per patient. Key output is total addressable market in dollars.

math.setup: US population × % chronic migraine sufferers × % severe (prescription-seeking) × annual revenue per patient
steps: Price per injection = $200; injections per year = 12 months / 2 months = 6
math.answer: $36B per year total prescription migraine market

questions.prompt: What is Botox's potential annual revenue from the migraine indication?
questions.guidance: Apply the projected market share range to the total addressable market.

math.setup: Total market size × Botox market share range

questions.prompt: What are the key considerations the client should assess before launching?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers three buckets: (1) Branding — the Botox brand has a cosmetic/controversial image that may deter migraine patients; shared branding creates risk exposure if side effects emerge in the larger migraine population. (2) Cannibalization — if perceived as the same product, the lower-priced migraine version may erode the premium cosmetic market; off-label use and price erosion are real risks. (3) Regulatory & market access — FDA may require different labeling and specialist-only marketing; injectable format faces patient aversion compared to oral alternatives; insurance formulary coverage is uncertain given only comparable (not superior) efficacy vs. generics.

brainstorming.prompt: What concerns should the client take into consideration before deciding to launch?

categories.name: Branding
ideas: Botox brand carries a cosmetic and somewhat controversial image that may deter migraine patients
Shared brand name creates risk exposure if a new side effect is found in either indication
Migraine market is much larger than cosmetic market, increasing adverse event probability and brand risk

categories.name: Cannibalization
ideas: Patients and physicians may view both products as essentially the same, undermining market separation
A lower price point for migraines could cause off-label cosmetic use at the migraine price
Price erosion in the cosmetic segment is a material risk

categories.name: Regulatory
ideas: FDA may require different labeling or limit the product to certain specialties
Separate marketing programs may be required for each indication
Approval timeline uncertainty ahead of the projected 2016 FDA date

categories.name: Market Access & Payer Dynamics
ideas: Insurance companies may not add Botox to formulary if efficacy is only comparable to generics
Migraine patients may be unable to afford out-of-pocket treatment
Injectable format faces inherent patient aversion relative to oral alternatives

categories.name: Strategy & Alternatives
ideas: Launching under a different brand name could allow separate pricing and messaging
Targeting a specific patient subpopulation with superior efficacy could strengthen the value proposition
Expanding to international markets could increase total market size

recommendation: The projected $36B prescription migraine market and $7B–$14B potential annual revenue for Botox make this a financially attractive market to enter
However, launching under the Botox brand with a lower price point risks cannibalization of the profitable cosmetic indication and exposes both products to shared brand risk
Recommendation: proceed with launch but consider a separate brand name to enable differentiated pricing, messaging, and risk management
risks: Cannibalization of the Botox cosmetic franchise if price and branding are not carefully managed
Insurance formulary rejection given only comparable efficacy to cheaper generics
Patient aversion to injectables may limit uptake relative to oral alternatives
Regulatory requirements may add cost and complexity via separate marketing and labeling
A serious adverse event in the large migraine population could damage the cosmetic brand
next_steps: Evaluate branding options including a new sub-brand or entirely separate brand name
Conduct payer research to assess formulary inclusion likelihood and reimbursement strategy
Define target patient segment — particularly subpopulations where Botox shows superior efficacy
Assess regulatory pathway and labeling requirements with FDA
Model cannibalization scenarios to quantify cosmetic market impact at various migraine price points
